doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

title: Punching in, tape heads and the move to digital
summary: Punch-in technique with sync heads, and his first digital project in 1983.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Isn’t that interesting because now we think — oh how primitive.

But at the time that’s — you worked with what you had. I can recall that exact scenario, overdubbing a part on a track that had things in it and I would watch the engineer and he would like — “boop boop” in and out.
Oh punch in and out. Right.
Punch in and out for sometimes two notes or something like that.

Yeah. Another potential destructive activity. Yeah. But tape recorders got, you know in the early — originally there was a delay between — because you have an erase head, a record head, and a play head. There were three heads. And they were in that order: erase, record, play. So the way they developed tape recorders, that record head also had the capability to play back for the other tracks that weren’t being recorded on. So that was called the sync head. But there was a slight distance between the erase head and the record/sync head. So you’d have to anticipate your punch to allow for that time lag. So anyway it got interesting.
How many years was it from then that you made the transition to completely digital?

Well digital didn’t happen until the 90s. We’re talking you know 25 years. Well no, actually mid-80s I guess digital started really happening. I did my first digital project, recorded two digital — I think it was in ’83. So but Pro Tools and those sort of things didn’t develop until the next decade.
